statement: If a straight line touch a circle, and from the point of contact a straight line be drawn at right angles to the tangent, the centre of the circle will be on the straight line so drawn.
heath_proof: For let a straight line DE touch the circle ABC at the point C, and from C let CA be drawn at right angles to DE; I say that the centre of the circle is on AC. For suppose it is not, but, if possible, let F be the centre, and let CF be joined. Since a straight line DE touches the circle ABC, and FC has been joined from the centre to the point of contact, FC is perpendicular to DE; [III. 18]therefore the angle FCE is right. But the angle ACE is also right; therefore the angle FCE is equal to the angle ACE, the less to the greater: which is impossible. Therefore F is not the centre of the circle ABC. Similarly we can prove that neither is any other point except a point on AC.

**Statement:** If a straight line touch a circle, and from the point of contact a straight line be drawn at right angles to the tangent, the centre of the circle will be on the straight line so drawn.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line DE touch the circle ABC at the point C, and from C let CA be drawn at right angles to DE, so that the adjacent angles ACD and ACE are each right (D1.10). We must show that the centre of the circle ABC lies on CA.

**Step 2.** Suppose it does not. Let F be the centre of the circle ABC, F not lying on CA, and join CF (P1).

**Step 3.** Since DE touches the circle ABC at C, and FC has been joined from the centre F to the point of contact C, FC is perpendicular to DE (3.18); therefore each of the angles FCD and FCE is right (D1.10).

**Step 4.** But the angle ACE is also right (Step 1). Therefore the angle FCE is equal to the angle ACE, since all right angles are equal to one another (P4). Likewise the angle FCD is equal to the angle ACD (P4).

**Step 5.** Now, since F does not lie on CA, the straight line CF is distinct from CA, and so CF falls within one of the two angles ACE and ACD which CA makes with DE at C. If CF falls within the angle ACE, then the angle FCE is a part of the angle ACE, and the whole is greater than the part (CN5), so the angle ACE is greater than the angle FCE; but by Step 4 they are equal, which is impossible. If instead CF falls within the angle ACD, then in the same way the angle ACD is greater than the angle FCD (CN5), while by Step 4 they are equal, which is impossible.

**Step 6.** Therefore F is not the centre of the circle ABC. Similarly we can prove that no point other than a point on CA is the centre. Therefore the centre of the circle ABC is on the straight line CA drawn from the point of contact at right angles to the tangent DE.

Therefore, if a straight line touch a circle, and from the point of contact a straight line be drawn at right angles to the tangent, the centre of the circle will be on the straight line so drawn. Q.E.D.
